21.0.s.en: (1) The dwelling of God with men

21.0.0.en: A new heaven and a new earth: that is, a vision of a new creation that men have not known before and that has not even entered our imagination.

21.0.1.en: It is noted that at the beginning of the Holy Bible (Gen 1) the discussion was about the creation of heaven and earth, and as the Holy Bible ends, the discussion is also about "a new heaven and a new earth," and to confirm this new picture of heaven and earth, he adds for us and affirms the passing away of the material earth and the heaven of stars on which and under which men were accustomed to live.

21.0.2.en: As for the reason for the existence of a new heaven and a new earth, it is a figure for a new life that has no relation to the laws of the old life, and perhaps the most important of its features is the constant presence of God in it, as we will understand from the following verses, so it is the spiritual heaven and earth, which befit the presence of God.

21.0.3.en: And there was no more sea: the sea points to division and disturbance, for it is what divided the dry land, and its high waves are a symbol of turmoil, agitation and lack of peace.. and the meaning intended is that in the Kingdom there is nothing of human conflicts or division.

21.1.0.en: I John: to confirm what is coming .. as when a person says, "I saw with my own eyes."

21.1.1.en: New Jerusalem: a symbol of the Kingdom of Heaven.

21.1.2.en: St. John continues his vision and declares to us that he saw the holy city of God, given as a gift by God (coming down from heaven), for the victors to inherit and enjoy; and to describe the intensity of its beauty, St. John found no more eloquent expression than that it is "a bride adorned for her husband," because it is known among people that the most splendid picture of a young woman is on the day of her wedding.

21.2.0.en: And in joy and gladness the heavenly creation announces, "a great voice out of heaven," that the most beautiful name for this great city is that it is "the tabernacle of God with men," that is, the place where God will bring together with men in permanent dwelling, where we all see Him "face to face" (1 Cor 13:12), and all will be the people and flock of God, while God is in the midst of all in the glory of His divinity, the source of eternal satisfaction and happiness.

21.2.1.en: "The tabernacle of God with men": the divine inspiration used the word "tabernacle" in describing the first church that God made in its finest details, which is the "tabernacle of meeting," because God wanted to declare to His people that He wants to dwell in their midst also, since the tent, the "tabernacle," was pitched in the midst of the tribes of the people of the children of Israel. And the Church also, "the tabernacle," is a permanent symbol of heaven, where man meets God in it, and the tabernacle of God with men is also a statement of the greatness of His love for the human race, for this is the pleasure of His heart, to be like a father among his children, and also a statement of His humility and condescension.

21.3.0.en: God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes: of course there will be no tears at all in the New Jerusalem, but it is enough for us to contemplate this beautiful scene that St. John portrayed for us, for Christ in the perfection of His tenderness stretches His hand over the face of each of us to wipe from our mind every memory of pain or weariness or distress that man passed through during his first life and his striving for the sake of God's name. And the scene, besides highlighting the tenderness of Christ, also shows how much God feels for us and does not forget the faithfulness of His children, and finally God confirms to us the idea of compensation with rest and happiness for the former pain; how wonderful is Your tenderness, my God, and the gentleness of Your feelings and Your justice and Your love for Your flock, O Good Shepherd.

21.3.1.en: The former things are passed away: a confirmation that the time of sorrows, pains and crying are all former things that have no place where there is endless happiness in the presence of God.

21.4.0.en: A direct command came from the Lord Christ, "him that sat upon the throne," to John to write His true and faithful words and promises, and they are words that confirm what was already indicated in the previous four verses, of the passing away of the old things and God's bringing of new things that we did not know before .. but they are the source of our eternal happiness.

21.5.0.en: It is done: this saying is Christ's, and its meaning is that He has already accomplished this new creation and prepared His Kingdom to receive His believing children after the judgment; and Christ used this expression twice, the first when He poured out His wrath on the wicked (16:17) and the second here when He glorified His children in the Kingdom. And the expression "It is done" reminds us also of our Savior's saying on the wood of the Cross, "It is finished" (Jn 19:30), and He means the completion of the redemption, which we receive in perfection in eternity.

21.5.1.en: Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end: an expression that Christ used in describing Himself in (ch. 1:8) at the beginning of the Book of Revelation, and it is an expression that concerns His divinity, for He is the source of all things and their Creator, and He is also the eternal, everlasting God.

21.5.2.en: I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely: these words remind us of the conversation of the Lord Jesus with the Samaritan woman "Jn 4," which she did not understand at first ... and the spiritual meaning here is that for all who thirst for righteousness and holiness (the water of life), Christ is the only source of their supply, whether this is during earthly time or in the time of absolute eternity ...

21.5.3.en: Freely: that is, a gift and grace from God, and this is in keeping with His love and fatherhood, for salvation was offered freely and all His graces to us are free, and likewise His spiritual gifts, but let us not forget that God is also just and does not forget all who rejected righteousness and sought evil.

21.6.0.en: He that overcometh: this expression was used in (ch. 2, ch. 3) with the letters to the bishops of the seven churches, and as a reminder here we say that this expression means:

21.6.1.en: a) The possibility of victory that was given by salvation to the children of God.

21.6.2.en: b) The necessity of victory for the inheritance and the enjoyment of the free gifts (the fountain of the water of life). Shall inherit all things: what God has prepared for His children who love His holy name and who overcome by the patience of their faith and their striving. I will be his: the Lord Christ moved here to the particularity of the relationship between each overcoming soul and its Christ, for after the discussion had been about the Christian people, "they shall be his people" (v. 3..), the words here are directed to each overcoming soul individually, so that the whole inheritance (all of heaven) becomes for each one, and every person becomes a distinguished son, as if he were an only son enjoying the fullness of his father's fatherhood ... and let us also notice the gentleness of Christ's expression in describing the relationship when He said "I will be his God," for He did not say he will be my servant but said son, which is the expression most in keeping with the fatherhood of God, who gives the inheritance not to slaves but to sons.

21.7.0.en: This verse makes clear the categories of those barred from the eternal inheritance and from the free gift of the water of life, whose portion is not in the heavenly Jerusalem but their destruction, "the second death," and endless torment in the lake burning with fire and brimstone... and these categories are:

21.7.1.en: (1) The fearful: what is meant here is not fear in the sense of anxiety for others or fear of animals or insects ... but what is meant is those who feared the world and the wicked, so they denied Christ and abandoned the faith for the sake of earthly life.

21.7.2.en: (2) Unbelieving: those who refused to believe in Christ and His free redemption and resisted His Church, for without faith it is impossible to please Him.

21.7.3.en: (3) The abominable: those who commit sins of impurity and did not repent of them.

21.7.4.en: (4) Sorcerers: those who used magic and the powers of evil and darkness and by this departed from God and became His enemy. (5) All liars: that is, those who went astray and led people astray ... and instead of doing the truth (the will of God in their lives) they did a lie (that is, they lied to themselves and to others.) And whoever lived his life in lying is none other than a child of the devil, for the Lord Christ says of Satan, "When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 8:44). (6) Idolaters: in its direct sense, whoever bows down to and worships idols, but in its spiritual meaning it is everyone who worships and clings to self or money..

21.7.5.en: God's love and fatherhood do not forget your weariness on earth and will compensate you for it with glories in heaven that cannot be expressed, so hold fast to your spiritual striving and endure the temporary pains of earth and do not be drawn after passing desires, and you will obtain the glories of heaven.

21.8.s.en: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

21.8.0.en: An angel appeared and spoke with St. John, whom the saint recognized in the Spirit, and he pointed out to us that he was one of the angels who carried the seven bowls of God's wrath (ch. 15), and the angel here was commissioned with a new mission, which is to show St. John the heavenly city. Just as this angel proclaimed God's justice in punishing the wicked with the bowls, here he proclaims God's justice in rewarding the righteous. He called the heavenly city the bride, as came in (v. 2), and declared that her bridegroom is Christ, a strong reference to the union of Christ (the Bridegroom) with His triumphant Church (the bride), and the angel used the name the Lamb here because it fits the Redeemer Bridegroom who bought the salvation of His Church with His blood.

21.9.0.en: He carried me away in the spirit: and this is in keeping with the state of St. John throughout the vision.

21.9.1.en: A great and high mountain: the expression here is symbolic, for it is customary among people to climb high summits so as to see the scene completely and comprehensively.

21.9.2.en: The purpose of the angel's taking St. John was to see the city in detail from all its sides and dimensions, and therefore the vision was from a high place so that nothing would escape him, and being high on the mountain symbolizes rising above earthly material things, because the heavenly city is entirely spiritual. And St. John repeats the same thing that came in (v. 2), that it is coming down from heaven from God (see the explanation).

21.10.0.en: Most precious stone: the greatest and most splendid stone.

21.10.1.en: Because of the intense beauty of the city (the heavenly Jerusalem), St. John could not portray this beauty for us in the limited language of men, so he used the expression "having the glory of God," that is, because it is His city and His Church and the place prepared before the foundation of the world for the children of God who inherit, and because it is the making of God Himself and His preparation, he ascribed to it His indescribable and unlimited glory, so that her honor is from the honor of God, and her standing and beauty surpass all imagination. And he added that it was very bright, with the brightness of a precious stone like the diamond in our present time, and this stone was also mentioned in the discussion of the throne of God (ch. 4:3), and the transparent, pure stone in its symbolic meaning indicates the purity of the Church's teaching and her firm faith and the virtues of her saints.

21.11.0.en: A wall great and high: the wall here has more than one significance or meaning:

21.11.1.en: 1- It signifies God's surrounding of His redeemed people in the city Himself, for God is the fortress and the refuge (Ps 43:2).

21.11.2.en: 2- The wall also signifies the one and only Church, for one wall surrounds the whole of the one city.

21.11.3.en: 3- The height of the wall, "high," signifies the exalted standing of the city, since in ancient times the greatness of cities was measured by the height and breadth of their walls.

21.11.4.en: Twelve gates: this statement agrees with what Ezekiel also mentioned in his vision (Ezek 48:31-34), and the existence of twelve gates (three gates on each side) is a reference to:

21.11.5.en: 1- The breadth of God's mercies, for if the way of striving on earth has a narrow gate, the heavenly reward has gates wide and spacious.

21.11.6.en: 2- The acceptance of the Gentiles from all races and from all quarters of the earth.

21.11.7.en: 3- The gates, like the wall, give a sense of security and guarding.

21.11.8.en: "Twelve angels": God put an angel at each gate, and this reminds us of "the overshadowing cherubim" on the ark of the covenant, and the presence of angels at the gates symbolizes care, protection and overshadowing for the people of God. The names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel: a reference to the entrance of the believers and saints of the Old Testament into this city, for God kept His covenant with His people and everyone who was faithful among them has a gate by which to enter eternity. The general meaning of the two verses (12, 13) is the acceptance of all believers from every direction and their enjoyment of the particular presence of God, "their wall," and the service of the angels to them.

21.12.0.en: Just as the believers of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel were accepted, so also the believers of the Church of the New Testament will be accepted, and everyone who received and took over the faith from the Fathers the twelve Apostles and from the Church. Twelve foundations: the names of the twelve tribes were written (v. 12) on the gates of the city, while the names of the Fathers the Apostles were the foundations carrying the city, and this is a clear reference that the foundation of the building of this heavenly city and of entering it is faith in Christ Himself, which was the foundation of the good news and preaching of the pure Apostles, and this is in keeping with what St. Paul the Apostle mentioned: "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone; in whom all the building fitly framed together) "... Eph 2:20, 21.

21.13.0.en: In (ch. 11) St. John was given a reed to measure the temple of God and the altar, but the one who measures here is the accompanying angel, and the purpose of the measuring is to highlight the glory, splendor and breadth of the city. A golden reed: the reed is the unit of measurement (like the meter), and its being of gold is to indicate the dignity of the city whose dimensions will be measured. There is another beautiful meaning, which is that spiritual (golden) things are measured only by spiritual things (a reed of gold.)

21.14.0.en: As for the description of the city as St. John saw it (and of course these are all spiritual, symbolic measurements and not truly material), it was foursquare, that is, the splendor of her glory is equal if a person looks at her from any side, and so is her height.

21.14.2.en: Twelve thousand furlongs: the material measure (two thousand two hundred and twenty kilometers) has no value here, but the purpose is to leave the reader's imagination to grasp the breadth of this city.

21.15.0.en: As for the height of her wall, it was (144 thousand cubits), and the number "144,000" has been repeated in the book twice, in (ch. 7:4) the number of "the sealed," and (ch. 14:1) "the followers of the Lamb," and in both cases this number was a figure for multitude, because it is the product of the numbers of perfection (12 x 12 x 1000), and consequently the height of the wall of the city here is a figure for the height of her glory beyond the imagination of any man.

21.15.1.en: The measure of a man, that is, of the angel: the human cubit equals about 50 cm, but the one who did the measuring is the angel, so the meaning intended is a spiritual one, that is, the great height and loftiness of this city.

21.16.0.en: After St. John mentioned that the foundations of the city are twelve foundations (the Apostles of Christ), he begins in the verses that follow to describe each foundation of them in terms of the stone it is made of and its color, with the meaning and spiritual reflections this carries.

21.16.1.en: First came in (v. 18) the general description, for the wall was of a precious stone, bright like the diamond, "jasper" (v. 11), and it is crystalline, that is, transparent, and likewise the city was of gold, which is a very precious metal, "pure," that is, without impurities or additions that reduce its value, but it is also not ordinary gold, for it is gold transparent as glass, in the sense that the brightness of the city and her glory does not hide or distract man from seeing God Himself. The first foundation, jasper: a transparent, shining stone inclining somewhat to green, and by its brightness and transparency it signifies the upright faith, and in its greenness eternal life.

21.16.2.en: The second foundation, sapphire: it signifies that the city is spiritual and heavenly and not subject to earthly measures.

21.16.3.en: The third foundation, chalcedony: a white stone that signifies purity and cleanness.

21.16.4.en: The fourth foundation, emerald: a green stone that signifies growth in grace.

21.16.5.en: The fifth foundation, sardonyx: it is white streaked with red, a symbol that purity is founded on the blood of Christ.

21.16.6.en: The sixth foundation, sardius: that is, it is built on the mystery of Christ's redemption (His precious blood.) The seventh foundation, chrysolite: the purest kind of gold, for everything in it does not rust (does not change or end.) The eighth foundation, beryl: it is the color of the calm, clear sea, and this is the state of the dwellers of the city of God. The ninth foundation, topaz: the topaz signifies enlightened insight.

21.16.7.en: The tenth foundation, chrysoprasus: life and its permanence (eternity.) The eleventh foundation, jacinth: sky blue, and its stone is very hard, a symbol of the immortality of the city and its dwellers.

21.16.8.en: The twelfth foundation, amethyst: a stone of purple color (dark red.) These stones and their colors have carried many spiritual reflections for many interpreters, but all agreed that nothing was meant by these stones except to highlight the wealth, virtue and grace that distinguish the city.

21.17.0.en: The foundations of the city (various stones) came as a reference to the various virtues that those who enter it must bear, but the gates came alike, a reference to the fact that entrance is by the one door of the sheep, single in its attributes.

21.17.1.en: The pearl: it is the stone hidden in the shell of the sea, and it signifies here the splendor of the glory of God that shines on the gates of the city, which had been hidden from us and has appeared.

21.17.2.en: The street of the city: that is, its middle and center, and it came like the description of her wall in (v. 18), that is, the gathering of the believers in it in great glory, which is symbolized by precious gold.

21.17.3.en: And in other translations the phrase "the street of the city" came in the sense of its square.

21.18.0.en: The temple is the symbol of God's presence and dwelling, and God in truth is not limited by a made or created place, and consequently there is no need for a temple, for in the heavenly New Jerusalem God the Father will always dwell, and His Son (the Lamb) will stand in His glory in her midst, and for this St. John used the expression that "the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it," that is, God shepherds His children in the Kingdom as a tender Father and as the Savior and Redeemer who loved them to death.

21.19.0.en: In the same way that he said that a temple is of no use, there will also be no sun or moon, first because they are among the requirements of earthly, temporal life and the old life that has ended, and second because there is no need of any light, since God is also her light and her splendor.

21.20.0.en: By the light of it: that is, the divine light of the city..

21.20.1.en: The children of God enjoy His light and walk, that is, grow in His knowledge and love, and this wonderful heavenly scene agrees with what Isaiah also mentioned: "And the nations shall walk in thy light, and kings in the brightness of thy rising ... they all gather themselves together, they come to thee" (Isa 60:3-5). The kings of the earth: the saints also come bearing their virtues and their former sufferings for the sake of faith, "their glory and honor."

21.21.0.en: Because God is her sun that never sets, there will be no darkness or night after this, nor any need to shut her gates.. for the gates were shut in earthly time to protect man from his enemies and to guard him from the fears of darkness, but now none of the old things has any place. The glory and honor of the nations: that is, the praise and glorification of all peoples and all nations for the name of the living, holy God.

21.22.0.en: There shall in no wise enter into it: of course, after the general judgment, the expression "shall in no wise enter into it" is meant to say that there will not be in her, for everyone who was "defiled or abominable" has his fate in the lake burning with fire and brimstone ... but the expression also carries to the reader a final reminder of the necessity of constant repentance on earth, for there is no place in the city for unrepentant sinners.

21.22.1.en: They which are written in the Lamb's book of life: that is, those whom the Lord Christ called to eternal salvation and who accepted this salvation and completed their striving and struggle against evil to the end, so that they have the great inheritance.

21.22.2.en: My beloved God, in Your love for us You wished to show a glimpse of the beauty of eternity and the splendor of the life that lasts with You and in Your presence, and despite the beauty of this glimpse, our human mind is still too limited to understand or imagine everything, but we trust in what St. Paul declared to us, that "Eye hath not seen ... which it is not lawful for a man to utter" (1 Cor 2:9, 2 Cor 12:4). I thank You, my God, for what Your hands have prepared for me even if I do not understand it now, but with St. Paul I desire that place and I desire to be with You always, for I believe that it is "far better" (Phil 1:23). The tree of life and the conclusion of the book: introduction to the chapter: verses (1-6) come completing the description of the city whose description began in the preceding chapter, while the remaining verses (7-21) come as the conclusion of the book and its various prophecies.
